claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase lamellar microstructure such as fcc/B2.
Internal lamellar boundaries in the initial alloy are prone to microcrack initiation.
A minor dopant introduced during processing will preferentially segregate to lamellar interfaces.
Dopant segregation will enhance the bonding and cohesion of lamellar interfaces.
Dopant segregation will increase the toughness of lamellar-colony boundaries.
Increasing local interfacial bonding strength will delay or prevent microcrack nucleation and propagation under tensile loading.
Tougher interfaces will improve load transfer across lamellar colonies.
Improved interfacial load transfer can simultaneously increase yield strength and tensile ductility.
The doped alloy will have higher yield strength than the undoped lamellar-colony baseline at room temperature.
The doped alloy will have higher ultimate tensile strength than the undoped baseline at room temperature.
The doped alloy will have higher room-temperature tensile ductility than the undoped baseline.
Interface doping will delay the onset of microcracking relative to the undoped baseline.
The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibits a strength-ductility trade-off under conventional processing.
The untreated baseline exhibits early microcracking at internal boundaries.
The intervention is beneficial only at dopant concentrations low enough to preserve bulk phase stability and lamellar morphology.
The beneficial effect is expected under room-temperature loading and may not persist at elevated temperature.

contradictions.description: The experiment describes the doped and undoped samples as having the same alloy composition, although adding an in-situ dopant necessarily changes the total chemical composition unless 'same composition' is intended to mean the same base composition before doping.
